title: AGROSORT AI
shortDescription: IoT-enabled robotic fruit-sorting platform built around a 4-DOF ESP32 robotic arm, conveyor system, web control interface, and computer-vision pipeline.

image.alt: AgroSort AI 4-DOF ESP32 Robotic Arm Setup

highlight: Built 4-DOF ESP32 robotic arm with web virtual joystick, Teach & Repeat sequence recording, and 6-class CNN fruit classification model (~90% accuracy).
result: 4th-semester robotic manipulation and web-control foundation completed; AI vision pipeline trained (~90% accuracy); full autonomous integration under active development.

caseStudy.overview: AgroSort AI is an IoT-enabled robotic fruit-sorting platform built around a 4-DOF ESP32 robotic arm, conveyor system, web-based control interface, and computer-vision pipeline. The project began with the physical robotic arm and its ESP32 control. A custom web control interface was then developed for remote arm operation, including virtual joystick control, keyboard control, position/state handling, and Teach & Repeat functionality. A CNN-based fruit-classification pipeline was subsequently developed as the AI component. The AI pipeline was developed separately and integration with the physical sorting loop remained an ongoing part of the project rather than being completely finished.
caseStudy.problem: How can a low-cost robotic system combine physical manipulation, conveyor-based material handling, web control, and computer vision to automate fruit sorting? During AI development, an additional integration problem emerged: a stationary fruit remained visible across consecutive camera frames, causing the vision pipeline to repeatedly classify the same physical fruit, creating the possibility of multiple sorting triggers for one object.
caseStudy.objective: Develop a prototype capable of controlling a 4-DOF robotic arm, controlling a conveyor, remotely operating the system through a web interface, recording/replaying arm positions/sequences, developing a vision-based fruit classification pipeline (~90% validation accuracy across 6 classes), and connecting the classification result to physical sorting.
caseStudy.myContribution: Developed and integrated the ESP32-based robotic-arm control system, web-based arm/conveyor control, and Teach & Repeat functionality; developed the CNN-based fruit-classification pipeline and worked on the communication/integration layer between computer vision and the physical ESP32 system; investigated duplicate-frame classification and hardware/software integration issues.
system: Hardware & Web Control: Web Control Center → (HTTP) → ESP32 (Wi-Fi AP) → 4-DOF Robotic Arm (Base GPIO 5, Shoulder GPIO 16, Elbow GPIO 17, Claw GPIO 18) + Conveyor (L298N Driver)
Separate AI Pipeline: USB Webcam → OpenCV Preprocessing → CNN Classification (6 Fruit-Condition Classes) → Classification Result → Integration Layer → ESP32 HTTP
development: Phase 1 — Physical arm: 4-DOF robotic arm controlled using ESP32 (Base GPIO 5, Shoulder GPIO 16, Elbow GPIO 17, Claw GPIO 18).
Phase 2 — Manual control: Web interface featuring virtual joystick, keyboard controls, individual joint control, and state representation.
Phase 3 — Teach & Repeat: Sequence recording and replay with Bin A / Bin B sequence storage.
Phase 4 — Conveyor integration: Conveyor control via ESP32 and L298N driver with web endpoints (/conveyor/start, /stop, /reverse, /speed).
Phase 5 — AI vision: Trained 6-class CNN pipeline (Fresh/Rotten Apple, Grape, Strawberry) reaching ~90% validation accuracy, exported to final_model.keras and model.tflite.
Phase 6 — Integration & Debugging: Connecting perception, classification, decision, and actuation without duplicate object triggers.
challenges: ESP32 Wi-Fi instability was observed during motor/servo operation under battery power. Power distribution, motor interference, and load-related behavior were investigated.
A stationary fruit remaining visible across consecutive camera frames caused repeated CNN classification events.
Connecting AI classification results across perception, application logic, network API, ESP32 controller, and physical robotic actuation.
decisions: Selected ESP32 as embedded controller for servo PWM, conveyor driver, Wi-Fi AP, and HTTP API interface.
Developed browser-based control center for remote HTTP-to-ESP32 execution instead of relying only on physical controls.
Chosen CNN approach with a focused 6-class fruit-condition scope rather than a massive multi-fruit model.
Separated AI perception (laptop/computer) from physical hardware control (ESP32) rather than forcing on-device ESP32 inference.
results: Verified 4-DOF ESP32 robotic arm control, web-based virtual joystick, keyboard controls, and Teach & Repeat sequence replay.
Verified ESP32 Wi-Fi AP architecture and HTTP-based browser-to-ESP32 communication.
Trained 6-class CNN model achieving ~90% validation accuracy, exported to .keras and .tflite.
Conveyor control architecture integrated via L298N driver.
caseStudy.currentState: ACTIVE DEVELOPMENT — 4th-semester robotic manipulation and web-control foundation completed; AI vision developed; full autonomous integration remains under development and the project is continuing into the next semester.
caseStudy.lessons: The project evolved from direct ESP32 robotic-arm control into a larger hardware–software–AI system. Building the physical control layer first exposed practical issues in servo behavior, power, communication reliability, and command handling. Adding computer vision introduced a second class of problems involving dataset quality, model behavior, repeated frame inference, and the boundary between AI decisions and physical actuation. The project demonstrated that integrating AI with physical robotics is substantially more complex than developing either component independently.

title: SENTINEL SAST ENGINE
shortDescription: AI-assisted Static Application Security Testing (SAST) engine analyzing Python code using TF-IDF, structural metrics, and security heuristics.

image.alt: Sentinel AI-Powered Python Vulnerability Detection Dashboard

highlight: Engineered structural code metrics (NLOC, complexity, nesting depth), security heuristics, and feature fusion with Word TF-IDF on CVEFixes data.
result: Trained calibrated Logistic Regression model with 92.50% vulnerability recall and developed Flask code & GitHub repository scanning endpoints.

caseStudy.overview: Sentinel is an AI-assisted Static Application Security Testing (SAST) engine designed to analyze Python source code for potential security vulnerabilities without executing the code. It supports pasted code, uploaded Python files, and multi-file GitHub repositories.
caseStudy.problem: Generic ML-based code classification can miss security-specific patterns and may produce false positives when analyzing complex source code. Sentinel addresses this by combining statistical code features with structural metrics and security-specific heuristics.
caseStudy.objective: Build a hybrid SAST engine that combines Word TF-IDF representations with structural code metrics and security heuristics to detect potentially vulnerable Python code.
caseStudy.myContribution: Engineered structural code metrics, contributed to the Logistic Regression ML pipeline using CVEFixes data, implemented security heuristics and guardrails, and developed Flask code and GitHub scanning endpoints.
system: Python Source → Code Preprocessing → Word TF-IDF + Structural Metrics + Security Heuristics → Feature Fusion → Logistic Regression → Calibrated Probability Threshold → Security Guardrail → Vulnerability Classification → CWE Mapping & Recommendation
development: Extracted and prepared vulnerability data from the CVEFixes dataset.
Implemented Python source-code preprocessing and feature extraction.
Engineered structural metrics including NLOC, cyclomatic complexity, token count, and nesting depth.
Added Word TF-IDF features and security-specific heuristic indicators.
Compared Random Forest and Logistic Regression model variants and selected the best-performing validation model.
Added probability-threshold calibration and deterministic security guardrails.
Integrated the analysis engine with Flask and GitHub repository scanning.
challenges: Text-based features alone cannot represent all structural and security-specific characteristics of source code.
The ML classifier produced false positives, requiring security-specific heuristic verification.
Vulnerability detection required balancing recall against precision through probability-threshold calibration.
decisions: Combined Word TF-IDF features with structural code metrics and security heuristics instead of relying on source-code text alone.
Compared Random Forest and Logistic Regression variants and selected Word TF-IDF + Logistic Regression based on validation performance.
Applied StandardScaler to the numerical structural features before feature fusion.
Added a calibrated decision threshold to prioritize vulnerability recall.
Added deterministic security guardrails to verify high-risk ML predictions and reduce unsupported vulnerability classifications.
results: Evaluated the final vulnerability classifier using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC.
Reported Recall: 92.50% and F1-score: 0.6416 at the evaluated operating point (Accuracy: 48.33%, Precision: 49.12%, ROC-AUC: 0.5298, PR-AUC: 0.5307).
The results showed a strong vulnerability-detection bias, with high recall accompanied by a substantial false-positive rate.
Implemented multi-file GitHub repository scanning with vulnerability-type identification and CWE mapping.
caseStudy.currentState: Academic implementation completed. The final system integrates ML-based vulnerability detection, structural code analysis, security heuristics, threshold calibration, and Flask-based code and GitHub repository scanning.
caseStudy.lessons: ML prediction alone was not sufficient for security-oriented code analysis. The project demonstrated the importance of combining machine learning with domain-specific features, deterministic security guardrails, threshold calibration, and software integration. The major lesson was that building a practical AI system requires engineering around the model, not just training the model.

title: FBG SENSOR + PINN RESEARCH
shortDescription: Physics-informed machine-learning investigation of Fiber Bragg Grating wavelength shifts under strain and temperature.

image.alt: FBG Sensor Physics Informed Machine Learning Setup

highlight: Analyzed experimental strain/temperature wavelength shifts; established baseline metrics MAE 0.38 pm & RMSE 0.43 pm.
result: Formulated physics loss constraints embedding thermo-optic equations into neural network training.

caseStudy.overview: A physics-informed neural network (PINN) research project investigating Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG) optical sensor wavelength shifts (ΔλB) under varying physical strain and thermal conditions.
caseStudy.problem: Classical optical models struggle to decouple simultaneous thermal and mechanical strain shifts without complex physical calibration.
caseStudy.objective: Integrate physical governing equations directly into neural network loss functions to achieve high-precision strain-temperature decoupling.
caseStudy.myContribution: Cleaned and processed experimental sensor data, built classical baseline evaluation models, and designed the physics-informed loss formulation in PyTorch.
system: FBG Sensor Data → Data Cleaning → Wavelength Shift Calculation → Classical Baseline → Physics-Informed Loss Formulation → PyTorch Training → Evaluation
development: Evaluated experimental measurements under strain-only, temperature-only, and combined conditions.
Formulated physics loss terms penalizing physical equation violations during backpropagation.
challenges: Inconsistent wavelength column naming across sensor runs
Unit conversions between microstrain and picometer shifts
decisions: Built standardized data cleaning pipeline before model input
Decoupled pure MLP baseline from PINN physics loss formulation for empirical comparison
results: Verified Classical Baseline: MAE 0.38 pm, RMSE 0.43 pm
Documented exact empirical baseline metrics prior to PINN loss integration
caseStudy.lessons: A model is only as meaningful as its data semantics, physical formulation, validation, and connection to real measurements.

title: HUFFMAN VS SHANNON-FANO ARENA
shortDescription: Interactive web platform for visualizing and benchmarking two classical lossless data compression algorithms.

image.alt: DAA Compression System - Huffman vs Shannon-Fano Arena

highlight: Built interactive tree visualizers, code dictionary generators, and microsecond performance benchmarking arena.
result: Created interactive educational web platform demonstrating greedy optimal coding vs top-down recursive partitioning.

caseStudy.overview: Developed an interactive web-based algorithm arena comparing Huffman coding (greedy, bottom-up priority queue) against Shannon-Fano coding (top-down recursive partitioning).
caseStudy.problem: Abstract algorithm concepts are difficult to analyze visually without real-time tree construction and empirical compression ratio comparisons.
caseStudy.objective: Build a zero-dependency web visualizer rendering prefix tree generation, frequency tables, generated codebooks, and microsecond execution timing.
caseStudy.myContribution: Implemented Huffman min-heap and Shannon-Fano recursive algorithms in pure JavaScript, built dynamic tree rendering logic, and created benchmark suite.
system: User Text Input → Character Frequency Analysis → Tree Construction → Prefix Code Generation → Compression Ratio & Microsecond Benchmarks → Interactive DOM Tree Render
development: Used performance.now() API for microsecond timing comparison.
Built responsive CSS tree rendering logic mapping parent-child nodes dynamically.
challenges: Handling edge cases like single-character input strings
DOM rendering bottlenecks on large text inputs
decisions: Implemented greedy Min-Heap for optimal Huffman tree generation
Used Vanilla JS without heavy external visualization libraries
results: Successfully benchmarked compression efficiency across varying text entropy levels
Demonstrated optimal prefix property of Huffman over Shannon-Fano
caseStudy.lessons: Two algorithms can solve the same problem while making fundamentally different design decisions, and those decisions affect solution quality.

title: AI VISION BOX COUNTER
shortDescription: A low-cost AI vision system that detects, tracks, and counts cardboard cartons and converts physical box movement into SKU-based inventory information for small and medium-scale logistics operations.

image.alt: AI Vision Box Counter System Interface

highlight: Trained custom cardboard-box YOLOv8 detector achieving 0.917 Precision, 0.847 Recall, and 0.895 mAP@0.5 over 20 epochs.
result: Built automated carton counting, SKU mapping, and inventory logging Streamlit dashboard for logistics automation.

caseStudy.overview: Developed a computer-vision-based logistics system for detecting and counting cardboard boxes using a custom-trained YOLOv8 model. The system evolved from an initial generic real-time object counter into a domain-specific detection, tracking, ROI counting, SKU mapping, inventory logging, and Streamlit dashboard workflow.
caseStudy.problem: Generic pretrained object-detection classes were not sufficiently suited to the cardboard-box counting problem. Object tracking could also produce unstable IDs when detections changed or boxes moved close together, creating a risk of incorrect counting. The project addresses this by developing a domain-specific detection and counting pipeline intended for practical use in small and medium-scale logistics operations.
caseStudy.objective: Develop and integrate a domain-specific YOLOv8 detection model with centroid-based tracking and ROI counting to automate cardboard-box counting and connect detected box quantities to SKU-based inventory records. The broader objective was to explore an affordable computer-vision automation layer that can support logistics operations without assuming expensive industrial vision infrastructure.
caseStudy.myContribution: Developed and integrated the custom cardboard-box detection pipeline, trained and evaluated the YOLOv8 model, implemented centroid-based tracking and ROI counting logic, and developed the Streamlit-based inventory dashboard and data-persistence workflow. Also worked through iterative testing of detection, tracking, counting, performance, and UI behavior to refine the overall system.
system: Camera Input → Custom YOLOv8 Detection → Object Tracking → ROI Counting Zone → Counted Cartons → SKU / Units-per-Box Mapping → Inventory Calculation → Batch Logging → Streamlit Dashboard
development: Started with a generic real-time camera and object-detection prototype.
Integrated pretrained YOLO detection and bounding-box visualization.
Added centroid-based object tracking.
Experimented with line-crossing counting for moving objects.
Shifted toward rectangular ROI-based counting for the logistics workflow.
Identified limitations of generic pretrained classes for cardboard-box detection.
Developed and trained a custom YOLOv8 detection model for the target domain.
Integrated detection, tracking, counting, SKU mapping, inventory logging, and dashboard functionality.
Added local persistence for SKU and batch/inventory information.
challenges: CPU inference latency reduced real-time processing performance on the development hardware.
Centroid tracking instability could produce new IDs when detections changed significantly or objects moved close together.
Generic YOLO detection limitations made the pretrained model unsuitable for reliably representing the target carton-counting problem.
Counting reliability depended on consistent interaction between detection, tracking, and ROI event logic.
UI integration required separating the live vision output from the larger inventory-management workflow.
decisions: Trained a custom YOLOv8 detector for the target cardboard-box domain instead of relying solely on generic COCO classes.
Tuned centroid-tracking distance and disappearance thresholds to improve object-ID stability.
Used ROI-based counting to convert tracked detections into discrete counting events.
Connected detected box counts to SKU and units-per-box mappings for inventory calculation.
Used Streamlit to provide the operator-facing dashboard.
Used lightweight JSON persistence for SKU and inventory/batch records in the prototype.
results: Trained custom YOLOv8 Model achieving Precision: 0.917, Recall: 0.847, mAP@0.5: 0.895 over 20 training epochs.
Model evaluation included training-loss analysis, precision-recall analysis, and a normalized confusion matrix.
Implemented ID-based duplicate-count prevention logic within the ROI counting workflow.
caseStudy.currentState: Completed academic prototype for low- and medium-scale logistics automation. Integrates custom YOLOv8 detection, real-time camera inference, centroid-based tracking, ROI-based carton counting, SKU mapping, units-per-box calculation, inventory logging, Streamlit dashboard, and local data persistence.
caseStudy.lessons: Domain-specific detection must be solved before optimizing downstream tracking and counting. The project demonstrated that a practical computer-vision system requires iterative validation across detection, tracking, event logic, performance, and application integration rather than treating model accuracy as the entire solution.
caseStudy.novelty: Provides a low-cost vision automation workflow for small and medium-scale logistics operations. Connects Physical Carton Movement → AI Detection → Tracking → Counting → SKU Mapping → Inventory Information as a lightweight alternative to workflows that otherwise depend heavily on manual counting or expensive industrial vision infrastructure.

title: ERDOS HEALTHCARE SIMULATION
shortDescription: DSA-based emergency healthcare workflow simulation for patient triage, resource management, and doctor allocation.

image.alt: ERDOS Healthcare Simulation Data Structures Architecture

highlight: Engineered problem-driven DSA architecture mapping patient triage to Priority Queues and hospital beds to Hash Tables.
result: Implemented core PatientNode, PatientList, insertion, search, and priority triage modules.

caseStudy.overview: ERDOS is a DSA-driven emergency healthcare simulation system designed to manage patient triage, bed allocation, and doctor scheduling using explicit custom data structures.
caseStudy.problem: Generic sorting visualizers lacked real-world utility; academic requirements demanded multiple distinct data structures solving genuine domain problems.
caseStudy.objective: Design an emergency department workflow where each data structure handles a specific operational bottleneck.
caseStudy.myContribution: Designed domain problem mapping, implemented custom PatientNode linked lists, priority triage queues, and modular Python package structure.
system: Patient Arrival → Symptom Processing → Priority Queue Triage → Bed Allocation (Hash Table) → Doctor Scheduling → Discharge → Telemetry
development: Evolved project from basic sorting concepts into emergency hospital simulation.
Built modular Python classes for custom data structure implementations.
challenges: Designing explicit roles for 6+ distinct data structures without artificial bloat
decisions: Used Priority Queue (Min-Heap) specifically for emergency severity triage
Used Linked Lists for chronological patient arrival audit trails
results: Implemented PatientNode, PatientList, insertion, deletion, and priority sorting core modules
Validated unit test suite for queue operations
caseStudy.lessons: The problem determined the data structures. Didn't force data structures into an arbitrary app; changed the app so each structure had a clear purpose.

title: TRIP — TECH-ENABLED RURAL IMPACT PLATFORM
shortDescription: Farmer-centric agri-supply-chain startup concept developed through field validation, consumer research, and pilot planning.
highlight: Conducted field validation across 29 farmers in Mulbagal/Kolar & ~180 urban consumers in Bengaluru; mapped 6–11 intermediary markups.
result: Designed direct apartment-cluster procurement pilot model eliminating middleman price volatility.

caseStudy.overview: TRIP (Tech-enabled Rural Impact Platform) is an agri-supply-chain product concept aimed at connecting smallholder farmers directly to urban consumer clusters.
caseStudy.problem: Farmer income instability and unpredictable market access caused by 6 to 11 intermediary layers between farmgate and consumer.
caseStudy.objective: Conduct empirical field research and design a streamlined direct-to-cluster procurement and logistics model.
caseStudy.myContribution: Led field research in Mulbagal/Kolar, interviewed 29 farmers and ~180 consumers, mapped supply-chain markups, and authored pilot strategy.
system: Farmers → Direct Procurement → Micro-Hub Logistics → Apartment Consumer Cluster → Digital Traceability
development: Mapped exact supply-chain friction points from farmgate to urban retail.
challenges: High perishability risks during cold-chain transportation
Unpredictable daily crop yields
decisions: Focused pilot strategy on high-density apartment clusters to consolidate delivery logistics
Incorporated pre-order demand forecasting to reduce unsold inventory
results: Completed field validation with 29 farmers and ~180 urban consumers
Documented 6-11 intermediary layer markup structure
caseStudy.currentState: Deferred / Concept-stage startup after 2 years of field validation.
caseStudy.lessons: Demonstrates taking an ambiguous real-world problem -> going into the field -> gathering evidence -> challenging assumptions -> redesigning the system.

title: GRAVITATIONAL BATTERY
shortDescription: A physical energy-storage prototype exploring solar-to-gravitational energy conversion through a lifted mass and controlled electrical recovery.

image.alt: Gravitational Battery Physical Solar Energy Storage Prototype Setup

highlight: Built a 1 kg / 0.6 m vertical tower physical gravity energy storage rig with Arduino position tracking, INA219 current sensing, and 17.93% measured efficiency at 1 kg.
result: Demonstrated physical solar-to-gravitational energy conversion and electromechanical recovery across 250g–1000g loads.

caseStudy.overview: The project explored solar-to-gravitational energy storage by lifting a 1 kg mass through a 0.6 m vertical structure. Solar energy powered the lifting mechanism, storing energy as gravitational potential energy. During descent, the rotating shaft drove DC dynamo motors to recover electrical energy and power an LED load. The system combined mechanical energy storage, electromechanical generation, and Arduino-based locking control.
caseStudy.problem: The main engineering challenges were mechanical friction, shaft instability, weight balancing, motor overheating, plastic gear failure, and unstable electrical output under different loads. The locking mechanism also required iterative redesign to achieve controlled positioning and release.
caseStudy.objective: Design and experimentally test a physical solar-to-gravitational energy-storage and electromechanical recovery system, and analyze how different lifted masses affected the resulting current, power, and efficiency.
caseStudy.myContribution: Led the project concept and development; worked on the lifting/descent mechanism, Arduino-controlled NEMA17 locking system, DRV8825 integration, potentiometer position calibration, multi-load testing, INA219-based electrical measurements, and output analysis. (Note: NEMA17 was used specifically for the locking/stopper mechanism; lifting/descent operation used DC dynamo motors with manual 6-pin DPDT switching).
system: 20W Solar Panel → DC Dynamo Motor / Lifting Mechanism → 1 kg Mass → Gravitational Potential Energy → Controlled Release → Dynamo Rotation → Electrical Output → INA219 Measurement / LED Load
Arduino UNO → DRV8825 → NEMA17 → Locking/Stopper Mechanism
Potentiometer → Position Feedback → Arduino Lock Control
6-pin DPDT + push buttons → Manual lift/descent control
development: Started with the gravitational-energy storage concept and early lifting experiments.
Explored a separate stopper mechanism for holding the shaft.
Developed a 3D-printed mechanical stopper.
Moved to a NEMA17 stepper + DRV8825 for more precise shaft locking.
Added a potentiometer for lock-position feedback and calibration.
Retained manual lift/descent control through DC dynamo motors, DPDT switching, and push buttons rather than forcing full Arduino control.
challenges: Mechanical friction during the energy-recovery cycle.
Shaft instability and weight-balancing issues.
Plastic gear stripping under mechanical loading.
Motor overheating under sustained load.
Unstable/noisy behavior at lower mass loads.
Electrical output varying with physical operating conditions.
Designing a reliable locking mechanism for the lifted mass.
decisions: Adopted a NEMA17 (17HS8401) + DRV8825 configuration for the shaft locking mechanism to obtain controlled positioning.
Used a potentiometer as position feedback for the locking system.
Retained manual lift/descent control using DC dynamo motors, 6-pin DPDT and push buttons.
Tested multiple masses (250 g, 500 g, 750 g and 1 kg) to study the relationship between mass and electrical output.
Used INA219 measurements for current/power analysis and empirical regression modelling.
results: Demonstrated physical mass lifting and gravitational energy recovery through dynamo generation across 250 g, 500 g, 750 g, and 1 kg configurations.
The 250 g configuration showed noisy/unstable behavior, while the 1 kg configuration produced the strongest documented performance (17.93% efficiency).
Derived empirical relationships: Current: I = 69.23m + 57.38 mA | Power: P = 331.0m + 289.5 mW | Efficiency: η = 19.44m - 1.51 %.
caseStudy.currentState: Retired / Legacy Engineering Prototype. Completed as an experimental prototype and archived. Mechanical and control concepts preserved for future vertical-lift or energy system applications.
caseStudy.lessons: Built a complete physical engineering loop across mechanical design → electronics → motor control → position sensing → energy conversion → measurement → experimentation → debugging → iteration. The project demonstrated that theoretical energy-storage concepts behave very differently once friction, mechanical stability, gear strength, motor heating, load balancing, and generator behavior enter the system.
